Let $N\ge4$ be even, let $N_2,N_3\ge3$, let $L_*>0$ be a length, and choose
$0<\varepsilon<1$. On $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ with dimensionless angular
coordinates $x^i$, set
$$
\widetilde h=L_*^2\bigl((dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2\bigr),\qquad \widetilde\sigma=0,\qquad \tau=0,\qquad \phi_N(x)=1+\varepsilon\sin(Nx^1/2).
$$
Take the vacuum branch with $\Lambda=0$ and $\rho=j=0$, so the conformal data
are $h=\phi_N^4\widetilde h$ and $K=0$. Use a periodic mesh with
$N_1=N$ and counts $N_2,N_3$ in the other directions. Put
$\Delta_i=2\pi/N_i$ and use nodes
$x^i_{j_i}=2\pi j_i/N_i$, $0\le j_i<N_i$, with indices wrapped modulo each
$N_i$. For $i=1,2,3$, let $\mathbf e_i$ be the $i$th standard basis vector of
$\mathbb Z^3$. For a scalar grid array
$f_{\mathbf j}$, use the centered periodic maps
$$
(\delta_i f)_{\mathbf j}:= \frac{f_{\mathbf j+\mathbf e_i}-f_{\mathbf j-\mathbf e_i}}{2\Delta_i}, \qquad i=1,2,3,
$$
with indices reduced modulo $(N_1,N_2,N_3)$, and apply them componentwise.
For reconstruction, partition each periodic coordinate circle into the
half-open cells
$$
C_{\mathbf j}:=\prod_{i=1}^3 \left[\frac{2\pi(j_i-1/2)}{N_i}, \frac{2\pi(j_i+1/2)}{N_i}\right)\pmod{2\pi},
$$
and assign every component on $C_{\mathbf j}$ its value at node
$\mathbf j$. This specifies the piecewise-constant map
$\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$ in the constraint-residual definition.
For the reported residual arrays use uniform dimensionless weights
$w_{\mathbf j}:=(NN_2N_3)^{-1}$ and the norm
$$
\| (\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta},\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta})\|_{\boldsymbol\Delta,2} :=\left(\sum_{\mathbf j}w_{\mathbf j} \left(|\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta}(\mathbf j)|^2+ h^{ik}(\mathbf j)\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta,i}(\mathbf j) \mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta,k}(\mathbf j)\right)\right)^{1/2}.
$$
This example reports one mesh only, with no refinement hierarchy or
convergence comparison.

The discrete residuals $\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$ and
$\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$ vanish at every grid node, so their stated
weighted norm is zero. However, the
continuum Hamiltonian residual at $x^1=\pi/N$ is
$$
\mathcal H(h,K)=\frac{2\varepsilon N^2}{L_*^2(1+\varepsilon)^5}>0.
$$
Thus a smooth high-frequency field can have the same samples and zero discrete
residual as flat data while violating the continuum constraint between grid
points. A small or vanishing grid residual alone does not certify continuum
constraint satisfaction or solution accuracy.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron in the laboratory frame. Its boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Omega$ has the outward unit normal $n$ on each open face, defined up to the edge set of surface measure zero. Use the SI conventions of this framework. In particular $E$ has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $H$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, $D$ has units $\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}$, $B$ has units $\mathrm T$, and a volume current density $J$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$.

For a real vector field $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the distribution defined by

$$\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$

As in the real graph space definition of the imported mathematical library, $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ consists of the $L^2$ vector fields whose distributional curl is represented by an $L^2$ vector field, with norm

$$\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as carried by that imported weak-derivative convention. Let $\varepsilon,\mu:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be measurable, essentially bounded, real symmetric coefficient fields, independent of time. Require constants $0<a_\varepsilon\le b_\varepsilon<\infty$ and $0<a_\mu\le b_\mu<\infty$ such that, for almost every $x\in\Omega$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$,

$$a_\varepsilon |v|^2\le v\cdot\varepsilon(x)v\le b_\varepsilon |v|^2,\qquad a_\mu |v|^2\le v\cdot\mu(x)v\le b_\mu |v|^2.$$

The coefficient units are $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, respectively. They define bounded symmetric multiplication operators on $L^2$. Define $D(t)=\varepsilon E(t)$ and $B(t)=\mu H(t)$. The spatially varying coefficient fields are explicit local model data; they are not inferred from the homogeneous material-closure postulate. Its constant symmetric branch is a special case.

A field $E:I\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is in $C^1(I;L^2)$ when it has a derivative in the $L^2$ norm at every $t\in I$ and that derivative is norm-continuous. $C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega))$ means norm-continuity into the graph space. A finite-energy model solution is a pair

$$E,H\in C^1(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)),$$

with $J\in C(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$, satisfying the adopted evolution equations as $L^2$ identities for each $t\in I$,

$$\varepsilon\,\partial_t E=\operatorname{curl}H-J,\qquad \mu\,\partial_t H=-\operatorname{curl}E.$$

Its stored field energy is the finite real number

$$W(t):=\frac12\int_\Omega\bigl(E(x,t)\cdot\varepsilon(x)E(x,t)+H(x,t)\cdot\mu(x)H(x,t)\bigr)\,d\lambda_3(x).$$

There are two alternative boundary models.

**PEC.** Perfect electric conductor means $E(t)\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ for every $t$, where $H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ is exactly the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ in the displayed graph norm. This closure definition is used; it is not replaced by an unproved identification with every possible trace kernel.

**Impedance.** A Green-compatible tangential boundary pair consists of measurable fields $E_\tau,H_\tau\in L^2(\Gamma\times I;\mathbb R^3)$ with $n\cdot E_\tau=n\cdot H_\tau=0$ almost everywhere and, for almost every $t$,

$$\int_\Omega\bigl(\operatorname{curl}H\cdot E-H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E\bigr)\,d\lambda_3=-\int_\Gamma n\cdot(E_\tau\times H_\tau)\,dS.$$

This Green identity is part of impedance admissibility; membership in $H(\operatorname{curl})$ alone does not assert that such an $L^2$ pair exists. Let $Y\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$ be a time-independent scalar surface admittance, in siemens, with $Y\ge0$ almost everywhere. The impedance law is

$$H_\tau=Y(n\times E_\tau)\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Gamma\times I.$$

Then $Y|E_\tau|^2\in L^1(\Gamma\times I)$ and is the nonnegative outward boundary-power density in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. No pointwise boundary trace of an arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ field is asserted.
statement.proposed:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron in the laboratory frame. Its boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Omega$ has the outward unit normal $n$ on the relative interior of each planar face; edge and vertex values will be irrelevant under the face-area convention below. Use the SI conventions of this framework. In particular $E$ has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $H$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, $D$ has units $\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}$, $B$ has units $\mathrm T$, and a volume current density $J$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$.

For the boundary integrals, let $\mathcal F$ be the finite family of relative interiors of the planar two-dimensional faces of $\Gamma$. Write $\lambda_2$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^2$, defined as the restriction of Lebesgue outer measure to its Carath\'eodory-measurable sets; under the assumed $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, this is a complete measure. For each face $F\in\mathcal F$, let $P_F$ be its supporting plane and fix a Euclidean isometry $\iota_F:\mathbb R^2\to P_F$. For every Borel set $A\subseteq\Gamma$ (a set in the sigma-algebra generated by the open subsets of $\Gamma$), define $dS_F(A):=\lambda_2\bigl(\iota_F^{-1}(A\cap F)\bigr)$. Any two choices of $\iota_F$ differ by an affine Euclidean isometry of $\mathbb R^2$ with absolute Jacobian determinant $1$, so the Borel change-of-variables formula makes $dS_F$ independent of that choice. Each face is bounded and lies in a finite rectangle in its plane, so $dS_F(F)<\infty$. Set $dS:=\sum_{F\in\mathcal F}dS_F$ on $\Gamma$. The edges and vertices have $dS$-measure zero and are omitted, so $n$ is the outward face normal $dS$-almost everywhere; its values on edges and vertices do not affect any boundary expression. Since $dS$ is finite and Lebesgue measure restricted to $I$ is sigma-finite, $dS\otimes d\lambda_1|_I$ is the unique sigma-finite product measure on $\Gamma\times I$, with rectangle values $dS(A)\lambda_1(J)$ for Borel $A\subseteq\Gamma$ and Lebesgue-measurable $J\subseteq I$. All boundary $L^p(\Gamma)$ and $L^p(\Gamma\times I)$ spaces and almost-everywhere statements use these measures.

Every cross product in the boundary formulas is the right-handed Euclidean cross product in the positively oriented orthonormal frame basis: for $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ and $v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, $u\times v=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\,u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\,u_1v_2-u_2v_1)$, as in the cross-product definition of this library.

For a real vector field $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the distribution defined by

$$\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$

As in the real graph space definition of the imported mathematical library, $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ consists of the $L^2$ vector fields whose distributional curl is represented by an $L^2$ vector field, with norm

$$\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as carried by that imported weak-derivative convention. Let $\varepsilon,\mu:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be measurable, essentially bounded, real symmetric coefficient fields, independent of time. Require constants $0<a_\varepsilon\le b_\varepsilon<\infty$ and $0<a_\mu\le b_\mu<\infty$ such that, for almost every $x\in\Omega$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$,

$$a_\varepsilon |v|^2\le v\cdot\varepsilon(x)v\le b_\varepsilon |v|^2,\qquad a_\mu |v|^2\le v\cdot\mu(x)v\le b_\mu |v|^2.$$

The coefficient units are $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, respectively. They define bounded symmetric multiplication operators on $L^2$. Define $D(t)=\varepsilon E(t)$ and $B(t)=\mu H(t)$. The spatially varying coefficient fields are explicit local model data; they are not inferred from the homogeneous material-closure postulate. Its constant symmetric branch is a special case.

A field $E:I\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is in $C^1(I;L^2)$ when it has a derivative in the $L^2$ norm at every $t\in I$ and that derivative is norm-continuous. $C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega))$ means norm-continuity into the graph space. A finite-energy model solution is a pair

$$E,H\in C^1(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)),$$

with $J\in C(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$, satisfying the adopted evolution equations as $L^2$ identities for each $t\in I$,

$$\varepsilon\,\partial_t E=\operatorname{curl}H-J,\qquad \mu\,\partial_t H=-\operatorname{curl}E.$$

Its stored field energy is the finite real number

$$W(t):=\frac12\int_\Omega\bigl(E(x,t)\cdot\varepsilon(x)E(x,t)+H(x,t)\cdot\mu(x)H(x,t)\bigr)\,d\lambda_3(x).$$

There are two alternative boundary models.

**PEC.** Perfect electric conductor means $E(t)\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ for every $t$, where $H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ is exactly the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ in the displayed graph norm. This closure definition is used; it is not replaced by an unproved identification with every possible trace kernel.

**Impedance.** A Green-compatible tangential boundary pair consists of measurable fields $E_\tau,H_\tau\in L^2(\Gamma\times I;\mathbb R^3)$ with $n\cdot E_\tau=n\cdot H_\tau=0$ almost everywhere and, for almost every $t$,

$$\int_\Omega\bigl(\operatorname{curl}H\cdot E-H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E\bigr)\,d\lambda_3=-\int_\Gamma n\cdot(E_\tau\times H_\tau)\,dS.$$

This Green identity is part of impedance admissibility; membership in $H(\operatorname{curl})$ alone does not assert that such an $L^2$ pair exists. Let $Y\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$ be a time-independent scalar surface admittance, in siemens, with $Y\ge0$ almost everywhere. The impedance law is

$$H_\tau=Y(n\times E_\tau)\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Gamma\times I.$$

Then $Y|E_\tau|^2\in L^1(\Gamma\times I)$ and is the nonnegative outward boundary-power density in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. No pointwise boundary trace of an arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ field is asserted.

On a flat boundary face with outward normal $n=e_z$, take a right-handed tangent basis $e_x,e_y$, with $e_z\times e_x=e_y$, and let $E_\tau=E_0e_x$ for $E_0\in\mathbb R$. For surface admittance $Y\ge0$, the boundary condition $H_\tau=Y(n\times E_\tau)$ gives $H_\tau=YE_0e_y$ and outward power

$$n\cdot(E_\tau\times H_\tau)=YE_0^2\ge0.$$

If the sign in the boundary law is reversed, $H_\tau=-Y(n\times E_\tau)$, the outward power is $-YE_0^2$; it is strictly inward when $YE_0^2>0$, so the same energy balance records power entering the domain.
statement.proposed:
Use the boundary geometry of the preceding finite-energy model, with $\Gamma=\partial\Omega$. On a flat boundary face with outward normal $n=e_z$, take a right-handed tangent basis $e_x,e_y$, with $e_z\times e_x=e_y$, and prescribe tangential boundary data $E_\tau=E_0e_x$ for $E_0\in\mathbb R$. For surface admittance $Y\ge0$, the boundary condition $H_\tau=Y(n\times E_\tau)$ gives $H_\tau=YE_0e_y$ and outward power

$$n\cdot(E_\tau\times H_\tau)=YE_0^2\ge0.$$

If the sign in the boundary law is reversed, $H_\tau=-Y(n\times E_\tau)$, the outward power is $-YE_0^2$; it is strictly inward when $YE_0^2>0$.

For the conditional energy consequence, suppose an actual finite-energy model solution exists on a nonempty open interval $I$ and bounded Lipschitz polyhedron $\Omega$: $E,H\in C^1(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega))$, $J\in C(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$, the two evolution equations of the preceding boundary model hold as $L^2$ identities, and tangential boundary fields $E_\tau,H_\tau\in L^2(\Gamma\times I;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfy its Green compatibility identity. Take $Y\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$, $Y\ge0$, as in that model. If the reversed law $H_\tau=-Y(n\times E_\tau)$ holds almost everywhere on all of $\Gamma\times I$, then the model energy $W(t)=\tfrac12\int_\Omega(E\cdot\varepsilon E+H\cdot\mu H)\,d\lambda_3$ obeys

$$W(t)-W(s)=-\int_s^t\int_\Omega E\cdot J\,d\lambda_3\,dr+\int_s^t\int_\Gamma Y|E_\tau|^2\,dS\,dr\qquad(s<t).$$

In particular, if $J=0$ and the last integral is positive, the stored energy increases. This conclusion is conditional on existence of a solution satisfying the reversed law.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a local Lagrangian four-form on an oriented smooth
four-manifold, with a chosen first-variation decomposition
$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)$. Let
$\xi$ be a smooth spacetime vector field that has a local flow acting on the
fields, and assume the Lagrangian is diffeomorphism covariant, meaning
$\delta_\xi\mathcal L=\mathcal L_\xi\mathcal L$ for
$\delta_\xi\phi=\mathcal L_\xi\phi$. Define the Noether current three-form

$$J_\xi:=\theta(\phi;\mathcal L_\xi\phi)-\iota_\xi\mathcal L .$$

Then

$$d_MJ_\xi=-E_\phi[\mathcal L_\xi\phi].$$

Thus $J_\xi$ is closed on solutions. On every star-shaped coordinate
neighborhood $U$, a solution has a local two-form $Q_\xi$ with
$J_\xi|_U=d_MQ_\xi$.
statement.proposed:
Let $M$ be an oriented smooth four-manifold, let $\pi:E\to M$ be the chosen
smooth field bundle, and let $\mathcal L(\phi)$ be a local Lagrangian
four-form for its smooth sections, with a chosen first-variation decomposition
$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)$. Let
$\xi$ be a smooth spacetime vector field with local flow $\Phi_t$. Suppose
there is a smooth local lift $\widetilde\Phi_t$ to fibre-preserving local
diffeomorphisms of $E$ over $\Phi_t$, with $\widetilde\Phi_0=\mathrm{id}$
and the local flow composition law. On the common domain define its induced
pullback action on sections by
$$ (A_t\phi)(x):=\widetilde\Phi_{-t}\bigl(\phi(\Phi_t(x))\bigr). $$
Write
$$\delta_\xi\phi:=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}A_t\phi,$$
the vertical field variation determined by this smooth family; at each $x$
it lies in $\ker(d\pi)_{\phi(x)}$, the tangent space to the fibre $E_x$.
In the tensor-field case where $A_t\phi=\Phi_t^*\phi$, it is the Lie
derivative $\mathcal L_\xi\phi$ defined by the local-flow derivative.
Assume the action preserves the chosen field domain, and assume covariance in the precise
sense $\mathcal L(A_t\phi)=\Phi_t^*\mathcal L(\phi)$ wherever both sides
are defined; thus its derivative satisfies
$\delta_\xi\mathcal L=\mathcal L_\xi\mathcal L$. Define the Noether current
three-form

$$J_\xi:=\theta(\phi;\delta_\xi\phi)-\iota_\xi\mathcal L .$$

Then

$$d_MJ_\xi=-E_\phi[\delta_\xi\phi].$$

Here a solution means a field configuration $\phi$ at which the Euler
functional vanishes, that is, $E_\phi[\eta]=0$ for every smooth variation
$\eta$ in its domain. Thus $J_\xi$ is closed on solutions. For every chart
$\chi:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ whose open image $V$ is star-shaped, a
solution has a local two-form $Q_\xi\in\Omega^2(U)$ with
$J_\xi|_U=d_MQ_\xi$.

Let $(\mathcal S,\Omega)$ be a specified smooth presymplectic solution space
and let $X_\xi$ be an admissible vector field generated by a specified
diffeomorphism parameter $\xi$ that preserves the boundary conditions. Define
the **charge-variation one-form**
$\alpha_\xi:=\iota_{X_\xi}\Omega$ on $\mathcal S$. It is **integrable on
$\mathcal S$** when there is a globally defined smooth function
$H_\xi:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R$ with $d_{\mathcal S}H_\xi=\alpha_\xi$; this
is the convention $\iota_{X_\xi}\Omega=d_{\mathcal S}H_\xi$. When a
finite-dimensional smooth parameter family is specified, a closed pullback
of $\alpha_\xi$ has local primitives on star-shaped coordinate patches;
global integrability on $\mathcal S$ is the stronger exactness condition.
statement.proposed:
Let $(\mathcal S,\Omega)$ be exactly a finite-dimensional smooth solution
manifold with its smooth closed two-form as specified in
[[def-gr-fx-admissible-phase-reduction]]. Let $M$ be the spacetime and
$\pi:E\to M$ the chosen field bundle. For a fixed smooth spacetime vector
field $\xi$ with local flow $\Phi_t$, suppose a smooth local lift
$\widetilde\Phi_t$ to fibre-preserving local diffeomorphisms of $E$ over
$\Phi_t$ is specified, with the local flow composition law. Define its action
on a field section by
$$ (A_t\phi)(x):=\widetilde\Phi_{-t}\bigl(\phi(\Phi_t(x))\bigr). $$
Assume the joint local action $(t,p)\mapsto A_t(p)$ is smooth, preserves the
selected solution manifold and boundary conditions, and induces maps
$A_t:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$. For
$p\in\mathcal S$, define the induced phase-space vector field by
$$X_\xi(p):=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}A_t(p)\in T_p\mathcal S.$$
In particular, the association $\xi\mapsto X_\xi$ is specified by the
lifted action and its preservation hypotheses; it is not inferred merely
from the name of a diffeomorphism generator. Define the one-form
$\alpha_\xi$ on $\mathcal S$ by
$$ (\alpha_\xi)_p(v):=\Omega_p(X_\xi(p),v),\qquad v\in T_p\mathcal S.$$
It is **integrable on $\mathcal S$** when there is a globally defined smooth
function $H_\xi:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R$ with
$d_{\mathcal S}H_\xi=\alpha_\xi$, using the convention
$\iota_{X_\xi}\Omega=d_{\mathcal S}H_\xi$. For a smooth map $f:P\to\mathcal S$
from a finite-dimensional smooth parameter manifold and a chart
$\chi:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ with $V$ open and star-shaped, if the
pulled-back one-form $f^*\alpha_\xi$ is closed on $U$, then its coordinate
representative $(\chi^{-1})^*(f^*\alpha_\xi)$ has a local primitive on $V$.
Here $m\ge1$; if $m=0$, every one-form on the chart is zero and is locally
exact.
Global integrability on $\mathcal S$ is the stronger exactness condition.

Let $M=\mathbb R_t\times\mathbb T^3$ with periodic spatial coordinates
$(x,y,z)$ of period one, orientation
$dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$, and flat metric
$g=-dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$. Write
$\mathrm{vol}=dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$. For one-forms, define the
Hodge map by
$$*dt=-dx\wedge dy\wedge dz,\quad *dx=-dt\wedge dy\wedge dz,\quad *dy=dt\wedge dx\wedge dz,\quad *dz=-dt\wedge dx\wedge dy,$$
and extend it linearly with smooth coefficients. Let
$\psi\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, let $\mu\ge0$ be a fixed real parameter,
and take
$$\mathcal L=-\frac12d\psi\wedge *d\psi-\frac12\mu^2\psi^2\mathrm{vol}.$$
All objects here are mathematical; no physical units or empirical
interpretation are assigned. At the base solution $\psi=0$, take smooth
commuting variations satisfying
$(-\partial_t^2+\Delta-\mu^2)\delta_i\psi=0$. The chosen potential and
current are
$$\theta(\psi;\delta\psi)=-\delta\psi*d\psi,\qquad \omega(\delta_1,\delta_2) =\delta_2\psi*d\delta_1\psi-\delta_1\psi*d\delta_2\psi.$$
On the oriented cut $\Sigma_t=\{t\}\times\mathbb T^3$, with finite smooth
singular cycle obtained by triangulating the unit cube, the integrated form is
$$\Omega_{\Sigma_t}(\delta_1,\delta_2) =\int_{[0,1]^3} \bigl(\delta_1\psi\,\partial_t\delta_2\psi -\delta_2\psi\,\partial_t\delta_1\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dy\,dz.$$
With coordinate Lagrangian density
$\frac12(\partial_t\psi)^2-\frac12|\nabla\psi|^2-\frac12\mu^2\psi^2$,
the canonical momentum density is $\pi=\partial_t\psi$, so this is the
canonical Cauchy-data pairing.
statement.proposed:
Let $\mathbb T^3:=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$ with quotient map
$q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3$, and let $M:=\mathbb R_t\times\mathbb T^3$.
The one-forms $dx,dy,dz$ on $\mathbb T^3$ are the forms descended from the
translation-invariant coordinate one-forms on $\mathbb R^3$; $\partial_x,
\partial_y,\partial_z$ denote their dual descended coordinate vector fields.
For $f\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, spatial derivatives mean derivatives of its
$\mathbb Z^3$-periodic lift to $\mathbb R_t\times\mathbb R^3$. Define
$$\nabla f:=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf),\qquad |\nabla f|^2:=(\partial_xf)^2+(\partial_yf)^2+(\partial_zf)^2,\qquad \Delta f:=\partial_x^2f+\partial_y^2f+\partial_z^2f.$$
Give $M$ the orientation $dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$ and flat metric
$g=-dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$, and write
$\mathrm{vol}=dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$. The constant-time cut
$\Sigma_t=\{t\}\times\mathbb T^3$ has orientation $dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$,
equal to contraction of $\mathrm{vol}$ with $\partial_t$.

Distinguish this geometric cut from its representing chain. Let
$i_t:\mathbb T^3\to M$ be the inclusion $i_t(p)=(t,p)$, with image
$\Sigma_t$. In positive affine coordinates on the standard simplex, put
$$T_3:=\{r\in\mathbb R^3:r_j\ge0,\ r_1+r_2+r_3\le1\}$$
with orientation $dr_1\wedge dr_2\wedge dr_3$. For each permutation
$\rho\in S_3$, put $v_0^\rho=0$ and
$v_j^\rho:=\sum_{k=1}^j e_{\rho(k)}$ for $1\le j\le3$, where
$e_1,e_2,e_3$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb R^3$. Define
$$a_\rho(r):=\sum_{j=1}^3r_jv_j^\rho,\qquad Q:=\sum_{\rho\in S_3}\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\,a_\rho.$$
Here $Q$ is a finite smooth singular three-chain in $\mathbb R^3$.
For a smooth map $f$, its chain pushforward means composition of each
simplex: $f_\#(\sum_jc_j\sigma_j):=\sum_jc_j(f\circ\sigma_j)$.
The representing chain in $M$ is
$$C_t:=(i_t\circ q)_\#Q=\sum_{\rho\in S_3}\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\,\tau_{t,\rho},\qquad \tau_{t,\rho}:=i_t\circ q\circ a_\rho.$$
Every simplex has the stated domain orientation and coefficient
$\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)$. The affine images are the six ordered-coordinate
regions of the cube. Adjacent regions have identical ordered face maps
and opposite signed face coefficients; on the exterior, opposite cube
faces have matching ordered face maps after $q$, again with opposite
coefficients. Thus $\partial C_t=0$. By saying that $C_t$ represents the
oriented cut $\Sigma_t$, we mean precisely that for every smooth three-form
$\alpha$ on $M$,
$$\int_{C_t}\alpha=\int_{[0,1]^3}(i_t\circ q)^*\alpha.$$
The right side integrates the coefficient relative to
$dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$. This equality follows by summing the six simplex
pullbacks with their orientation coefficients, as checked in step 3.1;
it invokes only this explicit cube decomposition. Restrictions of fields
and forms below are to the geometric cut $\Sigma_t$, whereas boundary
and chain-integration operations use $C_t$.

For one-forms, define the Hodge map by
$$*dt=-dx\wedge dy\wedge dz,\quad *dx=-dt\wedge dy\wedge dz,\quad *dy=dt\wedge dx\wedge dz,\quad *dz=-dt\wedge dx\wedge dy,$$
and extend it linearly with smooth coefficients. Let
$\psi\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, let $\mu\ge0$ be a fixed real parameter,
and take
$$\mathcal L=-\frac12d\psi\wedge *d\psi-\frac12\mu^2\psi^2\mathrm{vol}.$$
All objects here are mathematical; no physical units or empirical
interpretation are assigned. Let $u_1,u_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ satisfy
$$(-\partial_t^2+\Delta-\mu^2)u_i=0\qquad(i=1,2),$$
and define the smooth two-parameter field family
$\psi_{a,b}:=a u_1+b u_2$ on $P=\mathbb R^2$. At $(a,b)=(0,0)$ the base
solution is $\psi=0$; the commuting parameter variations are
$\delta_1\psi:=\partial_a\psi_{a,b}=u_1$ and
$\delta_2\psi:=\partial_b\psi_{a,b}=u_2$. The chosen potential and current
are
$$\theta(\psi;\delta\psi)=-\delta\psi*d\psi,\qquad \omega(\delta_1,\delta_2) =\delta_2\psi*d\delta_1\psi-\delta_1\psi*d\delta_2\psi.$$
On the oriented finite smooth singular cycle $C_t$ defined above, the
integrated form is
$$\Omega_{C_t}(\delta_1,\delta_2) =\int_{[0,1]^3} \bigl(\delta_1\psi\,\partial_t\delta_2\psi -\delta_2\psi\,\partial_t\delta_1\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dy\,dz.$$
The integral on the right is over the fundamental cube for the descended
three-form. The initial-data pair used here is
$(\psi|_{\Sigma_t},\partial_t\psi|_{\Sigma_t})$. Write
$\mathcal L=\mathcal L_{\mathrm{coord}}\,\mathrm{vol}$; then
$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{coord}}=\frac12(\partial_t\psi)^2-\frac12|\nabla\psi|^2-\frac12\mu^2\psi^2.$$
Define its canonical momentum density by
$$\pi:=\frac{\partial\mathcal L_{\mathrm{coord}}}{\partial(\partial_t\psi)}=\partial_t\psi.$$
Thus the displayed form is the canonical pairing of the variations of
$(\psi|_{\Sigma_t},\pi|_{\Sigma_t})$.

statement.proposed:
Let $M=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $(X^1,X^2,X^3,X^4)=(t,x,y,z)$,
orientation $dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$, and flat metric
$-dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$. For one-forms use
$$*dt=-dx\wedge dy\wedge dz,\qquad *dx=-dt\wedge dy\wedge dz,\qquad *dy=dt\wedge dx\wedge dz,\qquad *dz=-dt\wedge dx\wedge dy.$$
Here the massless wave equation means
$(-\partial_t^2+\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2+\partial_z^2)u=0$. Let
$u_1:=t^2+x^2$ and $u_2:=t$, and define the smooth field family
$\psi_{a,b}:=a u_1+b u_2$ on $P=\mathbb R^2$. Both $u_1,u_2$ solve the
massless wave equation, so $\psi=0$ at $(a,b)=(0,0)$ is a solution and
$\delta_1\psi:=\partial_a\psi_{a,b}=u_1$,
$\delta_2\psi:=\partial_b\psi_{a,b}=u_2$ are commuting variations solving
that same equation.
Use the massless scalar Lagrangian
$\mathcal L=-\tfrac12d\psi\wedge*d\psi$, with selected potential
$\theta(\psi;\delta\psi)=-\delta\psi*d\psi$ and current
$\omega(\delta_1,\delta_2)
=\delta_2\psi*d\delta_1\psi-\delta_1\psi*d\delta_2\psi$.
For $0<t_1<t_2$ and $L>0$, put
$a_0=(t_1,0,0,0)$ and
$(\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4)=(t_2-t_1,L,1,1)$. Let
$$T_4:=\{r\in\mathbb R^4:r_j\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_{j=1}^4r_j\le1\}$$
with orientation $dr_1\wedge dr_2\wedge dr_3\wedge dr_4$. For each
permutation $\rho\in S_4$, define vertices
$$v_0^\rho:=a_0,\qquad v_j^\rho:=a_0+\sum_{k=1}^j\ell_{\rho(k)}e_{\rho(k)}\quad(1\le j\le4),$$
where $e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4$ is the standard basis in the ordered coordinates
$(t,x,y,z)$. Define the 24 affine simplex maps and their oriented sum by
$$\sigma_\rho(r):=v_0^\rho+\sum_{j=1}^4r_j(v_j^\rho-v_0^\rho),\qquad
C:=\sum_{\rho\in S_4}\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\,\sigma_\rho.$$
Each map has domain orientation $dr_1\wedge dr_2\wedge dr_3\wedge dr_4$;
the coefficient $\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)$ orients it relative to
$dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$.

For $t\in\{t_1,t_2\}$, let $b_t=(t,0,0,0)$ and

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $U\subseteq M$ open. A **piecewise-smooth path** in $U$ is a continuous map $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$ for which some finite partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=1$ makes every restriction $\gamma|_{[t_{j-1},t_j]}$ smooth as a map of manifolds with boundary. Its source and target are $\gamma(0)$ and $\gamma(1)$. The collection of all such paths is a set: it is a subset, defined by separation, of the function set from $[0,1]$ to $U$.

Two paths $\gamma_0,\gamma_1$ with the same source $x$ and target $y$ are **thin-homotopic**, written $\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\gamma_1$, if there is a continuous map $H:[0,1]^2\to U$ and a finite subdivision of the square into compact curvilinear triangles such that $H$ is smooth up to each triangle's boundary, $H(0,t)=\gamma_0(t)$, $H(1,t)=\gamma_1(t)$, $H(s,0)=x$, $H(s,1)=y$, and $\operatorname{rank}(dH_{(s,t)})\le 1$ on every smooth triangle. A **curvilinear triangle** here is a compact region equipped with a smooth parametrization from the standard closed two-simplex, smooth up to its three edges. The rank is the dimension of the image of the differential from the two-dimensional tangent space of the triangle to $T_{H(s,t)}M$. The quotient by this relation is used only after its equivalence and compatibility properties are proved.
statement.proposed:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $U\subseteq M$ open. statement.before: For every smooth manifold $M$ and open $U\subseteq M$, thin homotopy is an equivalence relation on each set of piecewise-smooth paths with fixed endpoints, and concatenation respects the equivalence classes. $$U_{\partial R_\varepsilon}=I-\varepsilon^2F_{ij}(p)+O(\varepsilon^3),\qquad F_{ij}=\partial_i\omega_j-\partial_j\omega_i+[\omega_i,\omega_j].$$

Here the matrix norm is any fixed submultiplicative norm, and $O(\varepsilon^3)$ means its norm is at most $C\varepsilon^3$ for all sufficiently small positive $\varepsilon$, with $C$ uniform for basepoints $p\in K$.

Fix coordinate dimension $n\ge2$ and matrix size $q\ge1$, independently. Let $\omega=\sum_{k=1}^n\omega_k(x)\,dx^k$ be a $C^2$ $M_q(\mathbb R)$-valued connection one-form, with each $\omega_k:V\to M_q(\mathbb R)$. Along each segment use the matrix ODE $U'=-\omega(\dot\gamma)U$ and initial value $I_q$; existence and uniqueness for this fixed matrix size follow from [[prop-gr-fx-connection-path-transport-exists]]. For the tetrad connection of [[def-gr-fx-connection-path-transport]], take $q=4$. For $p\in K$, distinct coordinate directions $i,j$, and sufficiently small positive $\varepsilon$ so the square stays in $V$, define $\gamma_\varepsilon$ by traversing each straight side at constant speed over one quarter of $[0,1]$, in the order

$$p\to p+\varepsilon e_i\to p+\varepsilon e_i+\varepsilon e_j\to p+\varepsilon e_j\to p.$$

Its boundary orientation is positive for the ordered coordinate pair $(e_i,e_j)$.

$$U_{\gamma_\varepsilon}(1)=I_q-\varepsilon^2F_{ij}(p)+O(\varepsilon^3),\qquad F_{ij}=\partial_i\omega_j-\partial_j\omega_i+[\omega_i,\omega_j]\in M_q(\mathbb R).$$

A **finite oriented graph** consists of finite vertex and edge sets $V,E$, source and target maps $s,t:E\to V$, and a fixed-point-free involution $e\mapsto\bar e$ with $s(\bar e)=t(e)$ and $t(\bar e)=s(e)$. A **finite SU(2) graph configuration** assigns $g_e\in SU(2)$ to every oriented edge and requires $g_{\bar e}=g_e^{-1}$. A graph path is a finite composable edge word $e_1,\ldots,e_n$; its holonomy is the later-left product $g_{e_n}\cdots g_{e_1}$, and the empty path has holonomy $I_2$.

A vertex gauge assignment is a function $h:V\to SU(2)$. It acts on edge variables by

$$g_e\longmapsto g'_e=h_{t(e)}g_eh_{s(e)}^{-1}.$$

A **finite-dimensional unitary representation** is a continuous group homomorphism $\rho:SU(2)\to U(W)$ for a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $W$, where

$$U(W):=\{T\in\operatorname{GL}(W):\langle Tv,Tw\rangle=\langle v,w\rangle\text{ for all }v,w\in W\}.$$

For a closed graph path $\ell=(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$, the associated **Wilson trace** is

$$\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\rho(g_{e_n})\cdots\rho(g_{e_1})\bigr).$$

$$U(W):=\{T\in\operatorname{GL}(W):\langle Tv,Tw\rangle=\langle v,w\rangle\text{ for all }v,w\in W\},$$

with the operator-norm topology inherited from $\operatorname{End}(W)$. In finite dimension, strong continuity is equivalent to continuity in this operator norm.

$$\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\rho(g_{e_n})\cdots\rho(g_{e_1})\bigr).$$

$$W_v=\bigotimes_{t(e)=v}V_e\;\otimes\!\bigotimes_{s(e)=v}V_e^*,$$

$W:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, essentially bounded, and zero
almost everywhere outside a compact set. On $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ set
$H_0=-\Delta$ with domain $H^2$, $s=W^{1/2}$ as a multiplication operator,
and $H=H_0-W$ on $D(H_0)$. For $\kappa>0$ define
$$K_\kappa=s(H_0+\kappa^2)^{-1}s.$$
Then $H$ is self-adjoint and bounded below, and $K_\kappa$ is positive,
self-adjoint, and compact, with integral kernel
$$s(x)\frac{e^{-\kappa|x-y|}}{4\pi|x-y|}s(y).$$

isomorphic. Moreover, the finite number of eigenvalues of $H$ strictly below

multiplicity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H_0$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ with inner product linear in its first variable, bounded below, let $g\in\mathcal H$, let $\lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and put

$$P_gf=\langle f,g\rangle g,\qquad H_\lambda=H_0+\lambda P_g\quad\hbox{on }D(H_0),\qquad R_0(z)=(H_0-zI)^{-1}.$$

Adopt as an explicit conditional input the rank-one resolvent interface: $H_\lambda$ is self-adjoint, and whenever $z\in\rho(H_0)$ and $d(z):=1+\lambda m(z)\ne0$, where $m(z)=\langle R_0(z)g,g\rangle$, one has

$$(H_\lambda-zI)^{-1} =R_0(z)-\frac{\lambda R_0(z)P_gR_0(z)}{d(z)}.$$

Spectral variables use the energy unit of $H_0$. If $\|g\|$ is
dimensionless, $m(z)$ has inverse-energy units and $\lambda$ has energy
units; in general the coupling is chosen so that $\lambda m(z)$ is
dimensionless.

Let $E_\star\in\mathbb R$, take an open disk $D$ centered at $E_\star$, and let $E_\star$ lie in an open interval $I$ on which the spectral PVM $E_{H_0}(\cdot)$ of $H_0$ is absolutely continuous: $E_{H_0}(N)=0$ for every Lebesgue-null Borel set $N\subseteq I$. Suppose $m$ and, for specified test vectors $f,h$ in a subspace $X\subseteq\mathcal H$, the free matrix elements

$$\langle R_0(z)f,h\rangle,\qquad a_f(z):=\langle R_0(z)f,g\rangle,\qquad b_h(z):=\langle R_0(z)g,h\rangle$$

have holomorphic continuations through $E_\star$ to $D$. Suppose $d_{\mathrm{cont}}(z)=1+\lambda m_{\mathrm{cont}}(z)$ has a zero $z_0\in D$ with $\operatorname{Im}z_0<0$ of finite order $k\ge1$, and $a_f(z_0)b_h(z_0)\ne0$. Then the continued matrix element $\langle(H_\lambda-zI)^{-1}f,h\rangle$ has a resonance pole of order $k$. In the simple-zero case its residue is

$$-\frac{a_f(z_0)b_h(z_0)}{m_{\mathrm{cont}}'(z_0)}.$$

In particular, for the Gaussian model $H_0=M_{|p|^2}$, $g(p)=\pi^{-3/4}e^{-|p|^2/2}$, and $X=\operatorname{span}\{g\}$, the continuation in [[lem-nrqmx-gaussian-resolvent-continuation]] supplies $m_{\mathrm{cont}}$; every interval $I\subset(0,\infty)$ is absolutely continuous by the radial spectral measure formula. Every finite-order zero of $1+\lambda m_{\mathrm{cont}}$ in the lower half of such a disk gives a pole of the continued scalar element $\langle(H_\lambda-zI)^{-1}g,g\rangle$. These poles are not nonreal eigenvalues of the self-adjoint $H_\lambda$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\epsilon\le1$, and $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ with every partial derivative of total order at least $2$ bounded. Set
$$ h(x,\xi)=\frac{|\xi|^2}{2}+V(x),\qquad H_\epsilon^0=-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\Delta+V(x)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d). $$
Assume, as an explicit operator hypothesis, that for each $\epsilon$ a self-adjoint operator $H_\epsilon$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_\epsilon^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for $H_\epsilon$. Let
$$ U_\epsilon(t)=U_\epsilon(t,0) $$
be the unitary propagator supplied by [[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-common-domain-nonautonomous-evolution]] for the constant generator $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$. Define the global Hamiltonian flow by
$$ \dot x=\xi,\qquad \dot\xi=-\nabla V(x),\qquad \Phi_0=I. $$
For every $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and finite $T>0$, there is $C_{T,V,a}<\infty$, independent of $0<\epsilon\le1$, such that
$$ \sup_{|t|\le T} \left\|U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_\epsilon(t) -\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\right\|_{L^2\to L^2} \le C_{T,V,a}\epsilon^2. $$
Only fixed finite times are covered. No Ehrenfest-time, caustic-uniformity, or physical measurement conclusion is asserted. If $V$ is a polynomial of degree at most two, the difference is identically zero.
statement.proposed:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\epsilon\le1$, and $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ with every partial derivative of total order at least $2$ bounded. Set
$$ h(x,\xi)=\frac{|\xi|^2}{2}+V(x),\qquad H_\epsilon^0=-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\Delta+V(x)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d). $$
Assume, as an explicit operator hypothesis, that for each $\epsilon$ a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_\epsilon$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_\epsilon^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for $H_\epsilon$. Let $U_\epsilon(t)$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$; for $t<0$ it is the adjoint of the forward propagator at time $-t$. Define the global Hamiltonian flow by
$$ \dot x=\xi,\qquad \dot\xi=-\nabla V(x),\qquad \Phi_0=I. $$
For every $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and finite $T>0$, there is $C_{T,V,a}<\infty$, independent of $0<\epsilon\le1$, such that
$$ \sup_{|t|\le T} \left\|U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_\epsilon(t) -\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\right\|_{L^2\to L^2} \le C_{T,V,a}\epsilon^2. $$
Only fixed finite times are covered by the first estimate. No Ehrenfest-time, caustic-uniformity, or physical measurement conclusion is asserted. If $V$ is a polynomial of degree at most two, the difference in that branch is identically zero.

There is also an exact statement for every real quadratic phase-space Hamiltonian. Let $z=(x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^{2d}$, let $G=G^T\in\mathbb R^{2d\times2d}$, $\ell\in\mathbb R^{2d}$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, and put
$$ h(z)=\tfrac12 z^TGz+\ell\cdot z+c. $$
Set $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_d\\-I_d&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\widehat z=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,P_1,\ldots,P_d)$, where $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. On $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ define the Weyl realization by
$$ H_{\epsilon,h}^0:=cI+\sum_j\ell_j\widehat z_j+\tfrac14\sum_{j,k}G_{jk}(\widehat z_j\widehat z_k+\widehat z_k\widehat z_j). $$
For each $0<\epsilon\le1$, assume a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_{\epsilon,h}$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_{\epsilon,h}^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for it. Let $U_{\epsilon,h}(t)$ be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_{\epsilon,h}/\epsilon$. The global Hamiltonian flow, defined by $\dot z=J\nabla h(z)=J(Gz+\ell)$ and $\Phi_0(z)=z$, is
$$ \Phi_t(z)=e^{tJG}z+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)JG}J\ell\,ds. $$
Here $e^{tJG}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^n(JG)^n/n!$ is the matrix exponential.
Then for every $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$$ U_{\epsilon,h}(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_{\epsilon,h}(t)=\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t). $$

Assume Countable Choice, let $0<\epsilon\le1$, and use the one-dimensional oscillator
$$ H_\epsilon=-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{x^2}{2} $$
with its self-adjoint realization from [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]. For real $q,p$, the normalized Gaussian
$$ \psi^\epsilon_{q,p}(x)=(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/4} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-q)^2}{2\epsilon}\right) \exp\!\left(\frac{ip(x-q/2)}{\epsilon}\right) $$
has Wigner density
$$ W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](x,\xi)= \frac1{\pi\epsilon}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-q)^2+(\xi-p)^2}{\epsilon}\right). $$
Let $U_\epsilon(t)=e^{-itH_\epsilon/\epsilon}$, and define the evolved state's distributional Wigner functional on $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ by
$$ \langle W_t,a\rangle:=\langle \operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_\epsilon(t)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}, U_\epsilon(t)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\rangle . $$
Then it is represented by the exact density
$$ W_t(x,\xi)=\frac1{\pi\epsilon} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-q_t)^2+(\xi-p_t)^2}{\epsilon}\right), \quad q_t=q\cos t+p\sin t,\quad p_t=p\cos t-q\sin t. $$
Thus this quadratic model transports the Gaussian Wigner density exactly along its classical Hamiltonian flow; its phase-space covariance remains $(\epsilon/2)I_2$. This is a mathematical model calculation, not an experimental observation.
statement.proposed:
Assume Countable Choice, let $0<\epsilon\le1$, and use the one-dimensional oscillator
$$ H_\epsilon=-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{x^2}{2} $$
with its self-adjoint oscillator realization. For real $q,p$, the normalized Gaussian
$$ \psi^\epsilon_{q,p}(x)=(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/4} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-q)^2}{2\epsilon}\right) \exp\!\left(\frac{ip(x-q/2)}{\epsilon}\right) $$
has Wigner density
$$ W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](x,\xi)= \frac1{\pi\epsilon}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-q)^2+(\xi-p)^2}{\epsilon}\right). $$
Write $z=(z_1,z_2)=(x,\xi)$. For a measurable density $\rho:\mathbb R^2\to[0,\infty)$ with $\int\rho=1$ and $\int(|z|+|z|^2)\rho(z)\,dz<\infty$, define its mean and covariance by
$$ \mu_j(\rho):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}z_j\rho(z)\,dz,\qquad \Sigma_{jk}(\rho):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}(z_j-\mu_j(\rho))(z_k-\mu_k(\rho))\rho(z)\,dz. $$
This Wigner density has mean $(q,p)$ and covariance $(\epsilon/2)I_2$. On $\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ let $Qf(x)=xf(x)$ and $Pf(x)=-i\epsilon f'(x)$. For a normalized $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$, define $\bar Q_\varphi=\langle Q\varphi,\varphi\rangle$, $\bar P_\varphi=\langle P\varphi,\varphi\rangle$, $\Delta_\varphi Q=\|(Q-\bar Q_\varphi)\varphi\|_2$, and $\Delta_\varphi P=\|(P-\bar P_\varphi)\varphi\|_2$. These standard deviations satisfy $\Delta_\varphi Q\,\Delta_\varphi P\ge\epsilon/2$, and the displayed Gaussian attains equality with both deviations $\sqrt{\epsilon/2}$.
Let $U_\epsilon(t)=e^{-itH_\epsilon/\epsilon}$, and define the evolved state's distributional Wigner functional on $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ by
$$ \langle W_t,a\rangle:=\langle \operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_\epsilon(t)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}, U_\epsilon(t)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\rangle . $$
Then it is represented by the exact density
$$ W_t(x,\xi)=\frac1{\pi\epsilon} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-q_t)^2+(\xi-p_t)^2}{\epsilon}\right), \quad q_t=q\cos t+p\sin t,\quad p_t=p\cos t-q\sin t. $$
Thus this quadratic model transports the Gaussian Wigner density exactly along its classical Hamiltonian flow; its phase-space mean follows $(q_t,p_t)$ and its covariance remains $(\epsilon/2)I_2$. This is a mathematical model calculation, not an experimental observation.

Assume Countable Choice and $0<\epsilon\le1$. In the one-dimensional oscillator with $m=\omega=1$, $\hbar=\epsilon$, the normalized first excited state is
$$ \psi^\epsilon_1(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\epsilon}}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/4} x\,e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}. $$
Its Wigner function is
$$ W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_1](x,\xi) =\frac1{\pi\epsilon} \left(\frac{2(x^2+\xi^2)}{\epsilon}-1\right) e^{-(x^2+\xi^2)/\epsilon}. $$
It is strictly negative on the disk $x^2+\xi^2<\epsilon/2$. Consequently the assertion that every normalized pure state has a nonnegative Wigner function is false.

statement.proposed:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth surface with boundary. Let $D\subseteq M$ be a compact oriented region with the following local regularity: its interior points have disk charts, its smooth boundary points have half-disk charts, and each of its finitely many corners has a chart in which it is a quadrant or the complement of an open quadrant. Its boundary is a finite union of embedded $C^2$ arcs with pairwise disjoint interiors; each arc is the image of an injective $C^2$ parametrization with nonzero derivative, including one-sided derivatives at endpoints. Arcs meet only at their common endpoints, and at every corner their one-sided tangent vectors are linearly independent. Let $\eta=a\,dx+b\,dy$ be a complex-valued $C^1$ one-form on a neighborhood of $D$ in each local chart, where $C^1$ means its coefficients and first partial derivatives are continuous up to the boundary. Define $d\eta=(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)\,dx\wedge dy$ in each chart; the chain rule and symmetry of second derivatives make this expression coordinate-independent. Orient every open boundary arc outward-normal-first: $(\nu_{\rm out},\tau)$ is a positive basis of $TD$, where $\nu_{\rm out}$ is outward and $\tau$ is the positive boundary tangent. Integrals over $D$ use oriented coordinate Riemann integrals, and the boundary integral is the sum of the line integrals over its finitely many oriented arcs. Then
$$\int_D d\eta=\int_{\partial D}\eta.$$

$$\sigma_k^a:=I^{\otimes(k-1)}\otimes\sigma^a\otimes I^{\otimes(N-k)},\qquad J_k^a:=\tfrac12\sigma_k^a\quad(a\in\{x,y,z\}).$$

Let $d\geq1$ and $N\geq0$ be integers, let $V=\mathbb C^d$ with its standard
Hermitian inner product, and give $H_N:=V^{\otimes N}$ its standard
tensor-product inner product. For $\pi\in S_N$ use the left place action
$$\rho(\pi)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(N)},$$
and for $U\in U(d):=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A^*A=I\}$ use the diagonal action
$\Delta_N(U):=U^{\otimes N}$. For a partition $\lambda\vdash N$ with at most
$d$ rows, let $S^\lambda$ be the corresponding complex Specht module and put
$$M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,H_N),\qquad d_\lambda:=\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda.$$
Equip $S^\lambda$ with any $S_N$-invariant Hermitian inner product and equip
$M_\lambda$ with the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{M_\lambda}:=d_\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(g^*f).$$
Equip each $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ with the product inner product,
defined on elementary tensors by
$\langle s\otimes f,s'\otimes g\rangle=
\langle s,s'\rangle\langle f,g\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly, and give
the direct sum the orthogonal direct-sum inner product.
Then the evaluation map
$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\ \ell(\lambda)\leq d}S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda\longrightarrow H_N,\qquad \Phi(s\otimes f):=f(s),$$

and as the identity on $M_\lambda$, while every diagonal $U(d)$ action acts
as the identity on $S^\lambda$ and by postcomposition on $M_\lambda$. The
multiplicity spaces in the sum are nonzero; partitions with more than $d$
rows have zero multiplicity space.

statement.before:
Work in a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be the material region in that frame and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open time interval. The electric field $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, polarization fields $P_\ell:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, and magnetic fields $B,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial-vector fields in that frame. In SI, $E$ is in V m$^{-1}$, $P_\ell$ in C m$^{-2}$, $B$ in T and $H$ in A m$^{-1}$.

For a fixed finite integer $N\ge1$, adopt at every material point $x$ the constitutive equations

$$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}P_\ell(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t),$$

$$\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,t)+\gamma_\ell\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)+\omega_\ell^2P_\ell(x,t)=a_\ell E(x,t)\qquad (1\le\ell\le N).$$

Here $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ is a constant scalar with units F m$^{-1}$, $\mu>0$ is a constant scalar with units H m$^{-1}$, $a_\ell>0$ are constant parameters with units F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega_\ell>0$ are constant angular frequencies with units s$^{-1}$, and $\gamma_\ell\ge0$ are constant damping rates with units s$^{-1}$. The parameters are independent of position and time; this is the meaning of homogeneous in this model. The model is linear because all displayed field and oscillator relations are linear with fixed coefficients, and spatially local because the oscillator equation at $x$ uses only the field and oscillator state at that same $x$. The magnetic law has only the constant scalar coefficient $\mu$ and no independent magnetic polarization variable; this is the nonmagnetic oscillator model adopted here.

The word nonmagnetic here means that the oscillator sector has no dynamic magnetic response; the fixed scalar coefficient $\mu$ can still encode a separate static constitutive response. To identify the displayed quantities with the framework's macroscopic definitions, stipulate $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\varepsilon_\infty-\varepsilon_0)E+\sum_{\ell=1}^N P_\ell$ and $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\mu_0^{-1}-\mu^{-1})B$. Then $D=\varepsilon_0E+P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon_\infty E+\sum P_\ell$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mu^{-1}B$. This is a constitutive identification in the model, not a microscopic decomposition.

The oscillator state at a time $t_0\in I$ includes both $P_\ell(x,t_0)$ and $\partial_tP_\ell(x,t_0)$. For a causal zero-past response, the oscillator state vanishes before the declared onset of the applied field and the solution at $t$ depends only on that past field history. If $\gamma_\ell=0$, no decaying stationary impulse response is assumed; the zero-past branch is the retarded solution of the initial-value equation, not an absolutely integrable convolution for arbitrary bounded histories. This postulate does not assert that any actual material realizes the equations.

statement.before:
Use the finite Lorentz oscillator closure in its homogeneous material rest frame. Let $N\ge1$ be finite, with $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ in F m$^{-1}$, $a_\ell>0$ in F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega_\ell>0$ in s$^{-1}$ and $\gamma_\ell\ge0$ in s$^{-1}$ as in that model. Assume Countable Choice; for the strictly damped integrable-kernel dispersion clause also assume Dependent Choice, as required by the causal-response supplier. For the time convention $e^{-i\omega t}$, let $z$ denote complex angular frequency in s$^{-1}$ and define the absolute oscillator susceptibility, with units F m$^{-1}$, by

$$\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}(z):=\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}\frac{a_\ell}{\omega_\ell^2-z^2-i\gamma_\ell z},\qquad \varepsilon(z):=\varepsilon_\infty+\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}(z).$$

The dimensionless transfer function in the causal-response theorem is $\chi_{\mathrm{norm}}(z):=\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}(z)/\varepsilon_0$, so that it has the theorem's convention $P=\varepsilon_0\chi_{\mathrm{norm}}E$ for harmonic histories.

The function $\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}$ is analytic for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ for every $\gamma_\ell\ge0$. For real angular frequency $\omega>0$ in s$^{-1}$ away from undamped poles,

$$\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}\frac{a_\ell\gamma_\ell\omega}{(\omega_\ell^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma_\ell^2\omega^2}\ge0.$$

When every $\gamma_\ell>0$, each causal impulse-response kernel is exponentially decaying, satisfies the integrable-kernel hypotheses of the causal-response theorem, and $\varepsilon-\varepsilon_\infty$ obeys its unsubtracted Hilbert-transform relations. When $\gamma_\ell=0$, that oscillator's poles lie at $z=\pm\omega_\ell$ on the real boundary; the transfer function has no pointwise value at those poles, and no pointwise dispersion formula there is asserted. The theorem makes no universal group-velocity bound.

Let $d\geq1$, let $r\geq0$ be an integer, let $H=H^*\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ have units joules, let $\hbar>0$ have units joule-seconds, and let $L_1,\ldots,L_r\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ have units $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, with the finite GKSL convention of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. Put $K=-iH/\hbar-\frac12\sum_{a=1}^rL_a^*L_a$ and $R(u)=e^{uK}$ for $u\geq0$, with the exponential defined by its norm-convergent power series. For a density matrix $\rho\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, meaning $\rho=\rho^*\geq0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, define the no-jump branch at time $t\geq0$ by $W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)=R(t)$ and its branch state by $W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)\rho W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)^*$.

All time variables $u,t,s_1,\ldots,s_n$ are measured in seconds. For $n\geq1$, a jump-history label is $\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\{1,\ldots,r\}^n$ and its jump times are seconds $0<s_1<\cdots<s_n<t$. Define the corresponding branch operator by $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)=R(t-s_n)L_{a_n}R(s_n-s_{n-1})\cdots L_{a_2}R(s_2-s_1)L_{a_1}R(s_1)$ and the unnormalized branch state by $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)\rho W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)^*$. Its branch-weight density is $w_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)=\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)\rho W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)^*)$. The ordered-simplex integral of this density means the repeated Riemann integral $\int_0^t ds_n\int_0^{s_n}ds_{n-1}\cdots\int_0^{s_2}ds_1$, applied componentwise to matrices; each continuous real component is integrable on the compact integration interval. For $n\geq1$, $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-n/2}$ and $w_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-n}$; integrating over the $n$ time variables gives a dimensionless weight. If $r=0$, there are no branches with $n\geq1$. This definition alone does not assert that the branch weights sum to one.

Let $d\geq1$, let $r\geq0$ be an integer, let $H=H^*\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ have units joules, let $\hbar>0$ have units joule-seconds, and let $L_1,\ldots,L_r\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ have units $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, with the finite GKSL convention of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. Put $K=-iH/\hbar-\frac12\sum_{a=1}^rL_a^*L_a$ and $R(u)=e^{uK}$ for $u\geq0$, with the exponential defined by its norm-convergent power series. For a density matrix $\rho\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, meaning $\rho=\rho^*\geq0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, define the no-jump branch at time $t\geq0$ by $W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)=R(t)$ and its branch state by $W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)\rho W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)^*$.

All time variables $u,t,s_1,\ldots,s_n$ are measured in seconds. For $n\geq1$, a jump-history label is $\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\{1,\ldots,r\}^n$ and its jump times are seconds $0<s_1<\cdots<s_n<t$. Its branch-weight density is the real-valued scalar function $w_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)=\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)\rho W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)^*)$. For $n\geq1$, let $\overline{\Delta}_n(t)=\{(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\in\mathbb R^n:0\leq s_1\leq\cdots\leq s_n\leq t\}$ and $\Delta_n(t)=\{(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\in\mathbb R^n:0<s_1<\cdots<s_n<t\}$. Use the same formula for $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)$ on $\overline{\Delta}_n(t)$; it is continuous there because $R(u)=e^{uK}$ is continuous for $u\geq0$. If $V$ is a finite-dimensional real or complex vector space and $F:\overline{\Delta}_n(t)\to V$ has continuous coordinates in a basis, define $\int_{\Delta_n(t)}F(\mathbf s)\,d\mathbf s$ as exactly the repeated one-variable Riemann integral over the closed limits shown here $\int_0^t ds_n\int_0^{s_n}ds_{n-1}\cdots\int_0^{s_2}F(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\,ds_1$, integrating each real coordinate; for complex coordinates, integrate their real and imaginary parts separately. This value is independent of the basis because a change of basis is a finite linear combination and scalar Riemann integration is linear. For $V=\mathbb R$ this defines the scalar integral of the density $w_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)$; the same convention applies to branch-state integrands with values in $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and to integrands with values in the finite-dimensional complex vector space of complex-linear maps $M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$. The full recursion is well-defined for these arbitrary continuous integrands by [[lem-nrqmx-continuous-simplex-integrals]]: every inner integral is continuous in all remaining ordered parameters, so the next integral exists. That lemma also proves basis independence, linear-map commutation, the norm bound by the supremum times $t^n/n!$, and positivity for nonnegative real scalar integrands. Set $\int_a^a f(s)\,ds=0$ for a degenerate interval; hence every $n\geq1$ ordered-simplex integral at $t=0$ is zero. Let $\Delta_0(t)=\{()\}$ and define $\int_{\Delta_0(t)}F=F(())$; in the expansion, the $n=0$ contribution is the no-jump branch already defined above. For $n\geq1$, $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-n/2}$ and $w_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-n}$; integrating over the $n$ time variables gives a dimensionless weight. If $r=0$, there are no branches with $n\geq1$. This definition alone does not assert that the branch weights sum to one.

Work with finite-dimensional system and environment spaces $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$, where $d,m\geq1$, using the ordered tensor product $H_S\otimes H_E$ with the system factor first. A system or environment state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one; these state matrices are dimensionless. At the initial time, for every allowed system state $\rho$, adopt the joint preparation $\rho\otimes\eta$, where the fixed environment state $\eta$ does not depend on $\rho$. For each $t\geq0$, choose a declared unitary $U_t$ on $H_S\otimes H_E$, meaning $U_t^*U_t=U_tU_t^*=I$, with $U_0=I$. The reduced system dynamics is the map $\Phi_t(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left(U_t(\rho\otimes\eta)U_t^*\right)$, where for the fixed product basis the finite partial trace has entries $(\operatorname{Tr}_E R)_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{j=1}^mR_{(\alpha,j),(\beta,j)}$. This assignment excludes initially correlated joint states. It imposes no one-parameter group, continuity, or semigroup law on $U_t$.

A time-homogeneous finite GKSL model may instead be selected as a separate approximation: choose a fixed finite-dimensional Hamiltonian matrix $H=H^*$ in joules, a constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and finitely many jump matrices $L_a$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, and use $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ for $t\geq0$ with $\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_a\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right)$. Each application must state its rates and physical regime. Selecting this approximation is not a consequence of the finite unitary reduction, and this postulate claims no weak-coupling or reservoir limit.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $r\ge1$, let $H=\mathbb C^r$ with orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let $\mathcal F_s(H)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^{\otimes_s n}$
be the bosonic Fock space with vacuum $\Omega$ and creation and annihilation
operators $a_j^*,a_j$ from
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For
$N=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in\mathbb N_0^r$, set
$$|N\rangle:=\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{(a_j^*)^{n_j}}{\sqrt{n_j!}}\Omega.$$
Let $g_N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^r g_{n_j}(x_j)$ be the normalized product Hermite
function from [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]].
Then $(|N\rangle)_N$ and $(g_N)_N$ are complete orthonormal families, and the
map $\mathcal U|N\rangle=g_N$ extends uniquely to a unitary
$$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r).$$
On the algebraic finite-particle span, $\mathcal U a_j\mathcal U^{-1}$ and
$\mathcal U a_j^*\mathcal U^{-1}$ are respectively
$(x_j+\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ and $(x_j-\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ on product
Hermite functions. In particular the quadratures
$$Q_j=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j+a_j^*),\qquad P_j=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j-a_j^*)$$
act there as multiplication by $\sqrt\hbar x_j$ and as
$-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j}$, respectively. These are core identities;
they do not assert that a finite number cutoff preserves the canonical
commutation relations.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, an integer $r\ge1$, and an action scale
$\hbar>0$. Inner products are linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Use the Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary
$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\to L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ of
[[lem-nrqmx-finite-mode-fock-schr-identification]]. In Schrödinger coordinates
define the self-adjoint quadratures
$$Q_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt\hbar\,x_j)\mathcal U,\qquad P_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j})\mathcal U,$$
where $x_j$ is the real multiplication operator on its maximal domain and
$-i\partial_{x_j}$ is defined by conjugating that multiplication operator by
the unitary Fourier transform. Their common Schwartz core satisfies
$$[Q_j,Q_k]=[P_j,P_k]=0,\qquad [Q_j,P_k]=i\hbar\delta_{jk}I.$$
Write $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$ and
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
The Weyl unitary labelled by $z=(q_1,p_1,\ldots,q_r,p_r)$ is the unitary
whose grouped-coordinate formula, with $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$ and
$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)$, is
$$[W(z)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
It obeys $W(z)W(z')=e^{-i\hbar z^TJz'/2}W(z+z')$ and is regular and
irreducible. By the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem, every
nonzero irreducible regular Weyl system with this finite phase space and this
same nonzero central parameter is unitarily equivalent to it.

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$. For such a state define
$$d_j=\sum_nw_n\langle R_j\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle,\qquad V_{jk}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_nw_n \langle(R_j-d_jI)\psi_n,(R_k-d_kI)\psi_n\rangle.$$
These quantities are independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis in
each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))= \exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$
with real $d$ and real symmetric $V$. Here $R_j$ has units
$\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, each Weyl label has units
$1/\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, and $V$ has units of action. No finite particle
number truncation is used.

Use the finite-mode conventions, including their Axiom of Choice assumption, of the finite-mode symplectic-data definition. Let $r\ge1$, $\hbar>0$, and let $S$ be a real finite-mode symplectic matrix
in grouped order $(q,p)$ whose upper-right block $B$ is invertible. Consider
two unitary propagators $U_1,U_2$ obtained from time-dependent real
homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonians (no linear or constant term), both with
classical endpoint $S$. Use the normalization that each propagator starts at
the identity and solves the Schrödinger equation with Planck scale $\hbar$.
Precisely, on a compact interval $[0,T]$ with $T>0$, the real symmetric coefficient matrix $K$ is Lebesgue integrable entrywise, the classical path is the absolutely continuous solution of $\dot S(t)=J_0K(t)S(t)$ with $S(0)=I$, and
$$H_t=\frac14\sum_{a,b=1}^{2r}K_{ab}(t)(R_aR_b+R_bR_a),\qquad J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Here $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ has seminorms $p_{\alpha,\beta}(f)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$ for multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$. A unitary Schwartz automorphism is a unitary on $L^2$ restricting to a continuous linear bijection of $\mathcal S$ with continuous inverse. A normalized propagator is a path of these automorphisms with $U(0)=I$ such that, for each Schwartz vector, its trajectory is absolutely continuous in every Schwartz seminorm and obeys $i\hbar\,\partial_tU(t)f=H_tU(t)f$ almost everywhere. Absolute continuity for a curve means the usual finite disjoint-interval condition for its increments in each seminorm. These conventions include piecewise-smooth Hamiltonian paths.
Then
$$U_2=U_1\quad\text{or}\quad U_2=-U_1.$$
The same conclusion holds after multiplying both propagators by a fixed
normalized quadratic propagator, provided the resulting endpoint lies in a
chart with invertible upper-right block.
statement.proposed:
Use the finite-mode conventions, including their Axiom of Choice assumption, of the finite-mode symplectic-data definition. Let $r\ge1$, $\hbar>0$, and put $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix}$. In grouped order $(q,p)$, write
$$S=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R),\qquad A,B,C,D\in M_r(\mathbb R),\qquad S^TJ_0S=J_0,$$
and assume its upper-right block $B$ is invertible. Define
$$R_g:=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)^T.$$
Fix a compact interval $I=[0,T]$ with $T>0$. For each $j\in\{1,2\}$, let $K_j:I\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ have Lebesgue-integrable entries in grouped order and satisfy $K_j(t)=K_j(t)^T$ for every $t$. Let $S_j:I\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ be absolutely continuous with $S_j(0)=I_{2r}$, $\dot S_j(t)=J_0K_j(t)S_j(t)$ almost everywhere, and $S_j(T)=S$. Define the real symmetrically ordered quadratic operator on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ by
$$H_{j,t}:=\frac14\sum_{a,b=1}^{2r}(K_j)_{ab}(t)((R_g)_a(R_g)_b+(R_g)_b(R_g)_a),$$
with no linear or scalar term. Assume $U_j:I\to\mathcal U(L^2(\mathbb R^r))$ is a path of unitary Schwartz automorphisms with $U_j(0)=I$ such that, for each $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$, the path $t\mapsto U_j(t)f$ is absolutely continuous in every Schwartz seminorm and satisfies
$$i\hbar\,\partial_tU_j(t)f=H_{j,t}U_j(t)f$$
almost everywhere. Here a unitary Schwartz automorphism is a unitary on $L^2$ whose restriction is a continuous linear bijection of $\mathcal S$ with continuous inverse, and the Schwartz seminorms are $p_{\alpha,\beta}(f)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$ for multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$. Absolute continuity of each trajectory means the usual finite disjoint-interval condition for its increments in every seminorm. These hypotheses include piecewise-smooth Hamiltonian paths.
Then
$$U_2=U_1\quad\text{or}\quad U_2=-U_1.$$
The same conclusion holds after multiplying both propagators by a fixed
normalized quadratic propagator, provided the resulting endpoint lies in a
chart with invertible upper-right block.

Assume AC, $r\ge1$, and $\hbar>0$. Let $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$,
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
and let $W(z)$ be the regular irreducible Weyl system of
[[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. For every real
$S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$, there is a unitary $M_S$ on
$L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ such that
$$M_S^*W(z)M_S=W(S^Tz)\qquad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r});$$
equivalently, $M_S^*RM_S=SR$ on the common transported Schwartz core.
Any two such implementers differ by a scalar of modulus one. The same
construction applies in every nonzero irreducible regular representation
with this finite phase space and fixed central parameter $\hbar$, after the
unitary equivalence of
[[thm-nrqmx-finite-weyl-uniqueness-interface]].

There is also a connected topological group
$\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ of normalized propagators of real
homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonians on this finite-mode Schrödinger space.
Here a unitary Schwartz automorphism means a unitary on $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$
whose restriction is a continuous linear bijection of the Schwartz space
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ with continuous inverse. A normalized propagator
starts at the identity and solves $i\hbar\,\partial_tU(t)=H_tU(t)$ for a
real symmetrically ordered quadratic $H_t$ with no linear or scalar term.
Give $\operatorname{Mp}$ the topology of pointwise convergence of $U$ and
$U^{-1}$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ in its Schwartz topology; give
$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ its usual matrix topology.
The map
$$\pi:\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R),\qquad M\longmapsto S \quad\text{when }M^*W(z)M=W(S^Tz),$$
is a two-fold covering homomorphism. Its two points over $S$ act by $M_S$
and $-M_S$ when $M_S$ denotes either normalized lift; an arbitrary Weyl
implementer may differ from them by any scalar phase. This connected double
cover and its unitary action are the metaplectic group and metaplectic
representation. All mode counts here are finite; no infinite-mode
implementation claim is part of the statement.

Fix $s\ne0$. For each finite $N\ge1$, apply independently to $N$ vacuum modes
the one-mode dilation $[U_sf](x)=e^{-s/2}f(e^{-s}x)$. The
resulting finite-mode unitary exists, its mean total number is
$$N\sinh^2(s),$$
and the magnitude of its overlap with the $N$-mode vacuum is
$$|\langle\Omega_N,U_s^{\otimes N}\Omega_N\rangle| =(\cosh s)^{-N/2}\longrightarrow0.$$
These exact finite-$N$ calculations exhibit quantities that are not uniform
in mode number. They do not prove an infinite-mode non-implementability
theorem and do not assign a limiting density operator or measurement.

Assume Countable Choice, $m,\hbar>0$, and real $q,B$ with $qB\ne0$. On
$L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ close the nonnegative form
$$q_B[u]=\frac1{2m}\left(\|-i\hbar\partial_xu\|_2^2+\|(-i\hbar\partial_y-qBx)u\|_2^2\right),\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C).$$
Put $\omega_c=|qB|/m$,
$E_n=\hbar\omega_c(n+\tfrac12)$, and let $(\psi_n)_{n\ge0}$ be the
complete normalized eigenfunctions of the one-dimensional oscillator with
mass $m$, frequency $\omega_c$, and action constant $\hbar$ in its exact
self-adjoint oscillator realization. For
Schwartz $u$ define
$\mathcal F_yu(x,k)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-iky}u(x,y)\,dy$,
and use its unitary $L^2$ extension. Put $x_0(k)=\hbar k/(qB)$ and
$(Uu)(\xi,k)=\mathcal F_yu(\xi+x_0(k),k)$.
Then $U$ is unitary from $L^2(\mathbb R^2_{x,y})$ onto
$L^2(\mathbb R^2_{\xi,k})$. Writing
$$Uu(\xi,k)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n(k)\psi_n(\xi),\qquad f_n\in L^2(\mathbb R_k),$$
the form closure domain and value are exactly
$$D(\overline q_B)=\left\{u:\sum_{n=0}^\infty E_n\|f_n\|_{L^2(k)}^2<\infty\right\},\qquad \overline q_B[u]=\sum_{n=0}^\infty E_n\|f_n\|_{L^2(k)}^2.$$
Thus the form is the diagonal oscillator form with an unrestricted $L^2(k)$
degeneracy factor; it asserts no finite-area state count.

Assume Countable Choice, $m,\hbar>0$, and real $q,B$ with $qB\ne0$. Let
$c=\hbar^2/(2m)$, $\omega_c=|qB|/m$, and
$E_n=\hbar\omega_c(n+\tfrac12)$ for $n\in\mathbb N_0$. On
$L^2(\mathbb R^3_{x,y,z};\mathbb C)$ close the nonnegative form
$$q^{(3)}_B[u]=\frac1{2m}\left(\|-i\hbar\partial_xu\|_2^2+\|(-i\hbar\partial_y-qBx)u\|_2^2+\|-i\hbar\partial_zu\|_2^2\right),\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C).$$
Use the wave-number Fourier convention
$$\mathcal F_yg(k_y)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int e^{-ik_yy}g(y)\,dy,\qquad \mathcal F_zg(k_z)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int e^{-ik_zz}g(z)\,dz.$$
and set
$$U_3u(\xi,k_y,k_z)=\mathcal F_z\!\left[\mathcal F_yu\!\left(\xi+\frac{\hbar k_y}{qB},k_y,z\right)\right](k_z).$$
Then $U_3$ extends to a unitary map onto
$L^2(\mathbb R^2_{k_y,k_z};\ell^2(\mathbb N_0))$ by expansion in the
complete transverse oscillator basis $\psi_n(\xi)$. If
$$U_3u(\xi,k_y,k_z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n(k_y,k_z)\psi_n(\xi),$$
the form closure domain and value are exactly
$$D(\overline q^{(3)}_B)=\left\{u:\sum_{n=0}^\infty\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(E_n+ck_z^2\right)|f_n(k_y,k_z)|^2\,dk_y\,dk_z<\infty\right\},$$
$$\overline q^{(3)}_B[u]=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(E_n+ck_z^2\right)|f_n(k_y,k_z)|^2\,dk_y\,dk_z.$$

physical_scope.proposed: A nonrelativistic point-particle model with a static smooth external vector potential and locally integrable lower-bounded scalar potential on Euclidean R^d, d >= 1, in SI units. The planar field is the scalar perpendicular component and the three-dimensional field is the curl vector. The optional spin-half Pauli coupling is a three-dimensional effective model term only when its form is closable and semibounded; no measured g-factor or relativistic correction is asserted.

statement.before:
Use SI units with mass $m>0$ in kilograms, charge $q\in\mathbb R$ in
coulombs, action constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, vector potential
$A$ in tesla-metres, magnetic field $B=\nabla\times A$ in teslas, and
scalar potential-energy function $V$ in joules. For $d\ge1$ and smooth real
$A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, with real
$V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d)$ bounded below, adopt the minimal
coupling assignment whose core form is
$$q_{A,V}[u]=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\|(-i\hbar\partial_j-qA_j)u\|_2^2+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V|u|^2,\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C).$$
Use its closed form closure and the unique self-adjoint representing
Hamiltonian. For dimensional form norms use the fixed reference energy
$E_0=1\,\mathrm J$: apply the closed-form representation to
$q_{A,V}/E_0$ and multiply the representing operator by $E_0$.

For an optional spin-half degree of freedom in three dimensions, define
$$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S_j=\frac{\hbar}{2}\sigma_j.$$
For a core spinor $u=(u_1,u_2)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^2)$,
define the spin-independent form
$$q^{(2)}_{A,V}[u]=q_{A,V}[u_1]+q_{A,V}[u_2].$$
For a declared dimensionless real coupling $g$, adopt the effective Pauli core
form
$$q^{\mathrm P}_{A,V,g}[u]=q^{(2)}_{A,V}[u]-\frac{gq}{2m}\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(x)^*(S\cdot B(x))u(x)\,dx,$$
where $u^*$ is conjugate transpose and $(S\cdot B)(x)=\sum_jS_jB_j(x)$.
Include this term only in model instances where the resulting form is
closable and bounded below, and use its closed form closure and representing
Hamiltonian. No universal semiboundedness for arbitrary $A,V,g$ is asserted.
statement.proposed:
Use SI units with mass $m>0$ in kilograms, charge $q\in\mathbb R$ in
coulombs, action constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, vector-potential
components $A_j$ in tesla-metres, and scalar potential-energy function $V$ in
joules. For each integer $d\ge1$, let $A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$
be real and let $V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ be bounded
below. Adopt the general-dimensional minimal-coupling assignment whose core
form is
$$q_{A,V}[u]=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\|(-i\hbar\partial_j-qA_j)u\|_2^2+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V|u|^2,\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C).$$
Use its closed form closure and the unique self-adjoint representing
Hamiltonian. For dimensional form norms use the fixed reference energy
$E_0=1\,\mathrm J$: apply the closed-form representation to
$q_{A,V}/E_0$ and multiply the representing operator by $E_0$.

The magnetic-field notation is dimension-specific. In $d=2$, with coordinates
$(x,y)$ and $A=(A_x,A_y)$, define the scalar perpendicular field
$$B_\perp(x,y)=\partial_xA_y(x,y)-\partial_yA_x(x,y),$$
in teslas. Thus $A=(0,Bx)$ gives $B_\perp=B$ for a constant signed scalar
$B$. In $d=3$, for coordinates $(x,y,z)$ and $A=(A_x,A_y,A_z)$, define the
field vector $\mathbf B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ in teslas by
$$\mathbf B=(\partial_yA_z-\partial_zA_y,\ \partial_zA_x-\partial_xA_z,\ \partial_xA_y-\partial_yA_x)=\nabla\times A.$$
No magnetic-field object is assigned by this notation in $d=1$.

For an optional spin-half degree of freedom in three dimensions, define
$$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S_j=\frac{\hbar}{2}\sigma_j.$$
For a core spinor $u=(u_1,u_2)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^2)$,
define the spin-independent form
$$q^{(2)}_{A,V}[u]=q_{A,V}[u_1]+q_{A,V}[u_2].$$
For a declared dimensionless real coupling $g$, adopt the effective Pauli core
form
$$q^{\mathrm P}_{A,V,g}[u]=q^{(2)}_{A,V}[u]-\frac{gq}{2m}\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(x)^*(S\cdot\mathbf B(x))u(x)\,dx,$$
where $u^*$ is conjugate transpose and
$(S\cdot\mathbf B)(x)=\sum_{j=1}^3S_jB_j(x)$ for the three-dimensional
field vector just defined.
Include this term only in model instances where the resulting form is
closable and bounded below, and use its closed form closure and representing
Hamiltonian. No universal semiboundedness for arbitrary $A,V,g$ is asserted.

$q\ne0$ charge in coulombs, $B\ne0$ a constant signed magnetic field in
teslas, $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and $A(x,y)=(0,Bx)$ in SI units on
$L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$. Set $V=0$ and define the Hamiltonian by the
closed form of the core expression
$$q_B[u]=\frac1{2m}\left(\|-i\hbar\partial_xu\|_2^2+\|(-i\hbar\partial_y-qBx)u\|_2^2\right),\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C).$$
The resulting Friedrichs Hamiltonian is unitarily equivalent, under partial
Fourier transformation in $y$ followed by
