Fix a dimension $d\ge2$, a period length $L>0$ metres, and an equal particle mass $m>0$ kilograms. The position space is the flat torus $\mathbb T_L^d:=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$, with its quotient Euclidean distance. For each $N\ge2$ under consideration, let $\delta_N>0$ be the physical sphere diameter in metres and put $a_N:=\delta_N/L$. An admissible configuration $(q_1,\ldots,q_N)$ has pairwise torus distances strictly greater than $\delta_N$. For a hard-sphere trajectory below, require $\delta_N<L/2$; this restriction holds eventually in the scaling prescription. If two quotient displacement representatives of length $\delta_N$ existed, their difference would be a nonzero vector in $L\mathbb Z^d$, of length at least $L$, but the triangle inequality bounds its length by $2\delta_N<L$; thus the contact normal is unique.

A hard-sphere trajectory, when defined, has positions $q_i(t)\in\mathbb T_L^d$ and velocities $v_i(t)\in\mathbb R^d$ measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, with time $t$ in seconds. Positions are continuous and the position and velocity paths are piecewise $C^1$. Between isolated binary contacts, $\dot q_i=v_i$ and $\dot v_i=0$. A binary contact of particles $i,j$ at time $t_c$ means $\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T_L^d}(q_i(t_c),q_j(t_c))=\delta_N$, while no other pair is in contact at $t_c$. Write $v_i^-$ and $v_i^+$ for the one-sided velocity limits at the contact. Let $n$ be the unique unit vector from the centre of $j$ to the centre of $i$ along the shortest quotient displacement. The equal-mass elastic reflection rule is

$$v_i^+=v_i^- -\bigl((v_i^--v_j^-)\cdot n\bigr)n,\qquad v_j^+=v_j^- +\bigl((v_i^--v_j^-)\cdot n\bigr)n.$$

The Boltzmann–Grad scaling prescription is a sequence, indexed by all sufficiently large integers $N$, with $N\to\infty$, $a_N\to0$, and

$$N a_N^{d-1}=\kappa$$

for a fixed dimensionless $\kappa\in(0,\infty)$. Under this exact relation, $a_N=(\kappa/N)^{1/(d-1)}\to0$, so the trajectory restriction $\delta_N<L/2$ holds for every sufficiently large $N$. The factor $a_N$ is the diameter measured relative to the fixed box length, so the displayed parameter is dimensionless. This is a definition of a finite hard-sphere model and a scaling prescription only; it asserts neither global existence of the hard-sphere flow nor convergence to a Boltzmann equation.

Assume AC. Fix $\beta>0$ in reciprocal-energy units and a finite barrier height $B>0$ in the corresponding energy unit, so $\beta B$ is dimensionless; put $\epsilon=e^{-\beta B}\in(0,1)$, and let the five states be $\Omega=\{L_0,L_1,H,R_0,R_1\}$. The energies are $E(L_0)=E(L_1)=E(R_0)=E(R_1)=0$ and $E(H)=B$, so the Gibbs law is $\pi(x)=e^{-\beta E(x)}/(4+\epsilon)$. Let $Q$ be the symmetric proposal matrix specified by
$$Q(L_i,L_i)=Q(R_i,R_i)=\frac12,\quad Q(L_i,L_{1-i})=Q(R_i,R_{1-i})=\frac14,\quad Q(L_i,H)=Q(R_i,H)=\frac14\quad(i=0,1),$$
and $Q(H,x)=1/4$ for $x\in\{L_0,L_1,R_0,R_1\}$, with all other entries zero. Each row sums to one. Apply the Metropolis–Hastings procedure with target $\pi$ and proposal $Q$, and denote its transition matrix by $P$. Write $L=\{L_0,L_1\}$ for the left well and define
$$d(t)=\max_{x\in\Omega}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\rm TV},\qquad \|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}=\frac12\sum_{x\in\Omega}|\mu(x)-\nu(x)|.$$
The Gibbs law is invariant, but the chain started with law $\pi(\cdot\mid L)$ has probability $(1-\epsilon/4)^t$ of making no exit from $L$ during its first $t$ steps. Conditional on no exit, its two-state within-well transition flips between $L_0$ and $L_1$ with probability $1/(4-\epsilon)$; the conditional stationary law within the well is uniform, and from either state its within-well total-variation error after $t$ such updates is at most $\frac12((2-\epsilon)/(4-\epsilon))^t\leq2^{-t-1}$. Nevertheless,
$$d(t)\geq(1-\epsilon/4)^t-\frac{2}{4+\epsilon}\geq\frac14\qquad\text{for every integer }0\leq t\leq\lfloor\epsilon^{-1}\rfloor.$$
Thus the conventional worst-start mixing time $t_{\rm mix}(1/8):=\min\{t:d(t)\leq1/8\}$ exceeds $\lfloor e^{\beta B}\rfloor$, even though the chain can equilibrate quickly within one well. This is an exact finite mathematical example; it reports no simulated or measured data.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$S:D(S)\subseteq H\to H$ be a densely defined closable antilinear operator.
Its graph closure $\overline S$ is closed and has the polar decomposition
$$\overline S=J|\overline S|,\qquad |\overline S|=(\overline S^{\,*}\overline S)^{1/2}.$$
Here $J$ is antilinear, vanishes on $\ker\overline S$, and is isometric on
$(\ker\overline S)^\perp$; if $\overline S$ is injective and has dense range,
$J$ is antiunitary.

For a concrete von Neumann algebra $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ and a vector
$\Omega$ cyclic and separating for $M$, define
$D(S_0)=M\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$. Then $S_0$ is
well defined, densely defined, antilinear, and closable.

For this item, let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$S:D(S)\subseteq H\to H$ be an antilinear operator. Set
$$\Gamma(S):=\{(x,Sx):x\in D(S)\}\subseteq H\oplus H,$$
where $H\oplus H$ has its direct-sum Hilbert norm. Use the conjugate space
$\overline H$, canonical conjugate-linear surjective isometry $c_H:H\to\overline H$,
and linearization $\widetilde S:D(\widetilde S)\subseteq\overline H\to H$ from the earlier
conjugate-Hilbert-space and antilinear-adjoint definition. The map
$c_H\oplus I_H:H\oplus H\to\overline H\oplus H$ given by
$(x,y)\mapsto(c_Hx,y)$, with $I_H$ the identity on $H$, is a real-linear
isometric bijection and sends
$\Gamma(S)$ onto $\Gamma(\widetilde S)$. Call $S$ **closed** or
**closable** when $\widetilde S$ is closed or closable, respectively, in the
complex-linear sense already defined for densely defined operators.
For closable $S$, $\overline S$ denotes the antilinear operator whose graph is
the norm closure of $\Gamma(S)$; the proof verifies that this closure is a
graph and equivalently that $\widetilde{\overline S}$ is the graph closure
of $\widetilde S$. An **antiunitary** on $H$ means a conjugate-linear,
surjective isometry $H\to H$.
